blocks.x: Now when I start, you're going to start to ask me a question. All I can say is this is Octave Crosby. This is Octave Crosby, a piano player from New Orleans, Louisiana.
Now where were you born? What part of the city?
I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, in the 13th Ward. Where is that?
I don't know.
That's way uptown. Way uptown, way up above Napoleon Avenue.
Remember about what street it was?
Yeah, that was on Line and Waters.
What was the date, your birth date?
On the 10th of June, 1898.
Did your parents play any instrument, any musical family?

No, only one in the family. The only one? Only one that played music. Did you have any brothers or sisters that played? No brothers or sisters. I just didn't get up myself. Who was your first teacher? Well my first teacher was a lady by the name of Camilla Todd.
And by the way, did you start on piano or any other instrument?
No, I started on, I played drum at one time. First? Before you took up piano? Yeah, I took up piano. And then uh…
Tell me about that.

Yeah, I played drum before I picked up piano. Then I started to fool, my mother bought me a piano, that's been many years ago. And I started to fool around with the piano and uh… That's before I ever take any kind of lessons. I mostly learnt myself, you know what I mean, by air, voice. Yeah. And then uh… After I started to improve on the piano, I got hired more on piano than I did drums. So I decided to stick to the piano.
When you started on drums, did you just pick that up yourself?
Picked that up myself. Mm-hmm. I picked that up myself.
Did your folks get you the drum set or did you have to earn it yourself or how did you get it?
No, no, they bought me something. They bought me the piano and also the drums. Yes.
So they encouraged you then to take up music?
Well, I mean, I liked it myself, you see. And I used to beat on the steps, you know, with drum sticks, you know, with my steps. So they noticed that, so they bought me a set of drums and then…
Did you take any lessons at all on drums?
Not at drums, no. I take lessons at piano.
Mm-hmm. Now tell me about your teacher on piano.
Well, uh… A lady by name is Camilla Todd. How was that spelled?
That's Camilla?
T-O-double-D.
Yeah, and the first name…
C-A-M-I-double-L-A.
Mm-hmm.

And she used to play in the church at the First Street Baptist Church. That's the First Street Drive. Oh, that's the first town. Yeah. And I take lessons under her and I take lessons under another lady by name was Miss DeVoyne. Massey DeVoyne. I've heard her name. She used to live on Pusha Street. Mm-hmm.
Did either one of them ever play any dance music or just…

Oh, yeah. Camilla Todd played a lot of dance music years ago. Yeah, she used to play at the country club out there years ago. Yeah, she used to play the trumpet player by the name of Hippolyte Charles. Oh, yeah. He called him Hippolyte Charles. Exactly. On the way back, Joe Howard, fella called Joe Howard. I know him very well, yeah. He's dead now.
Yeah, she played the trumpet and the trubus.
That's right. Is that right? He played trumpet, yeah. Mm-hmm.
What did your teacher teach you? Did she teach you just regular classical music or dance music or what kind of a book did you use?
Well, she used the first grade of standard. The standard grade. Yeah, the standard grade. She taught you to read right away.
Yeah, she taught me to read.

That's right. Taught me to read. I just, I'd already knew how to play by ear, you know what I mean? I played by ear a long time. Piano? Yeah. What you did before that? I didn't know. You picked it up. Yeah, I picked it up, you see, on the piano. I played by ear a long time before I ever started the music.
Ever play any jobs by ear? Had you played by ear?
Yeah, sure. Before you took lessons? Before I took lessons, sure. Yeah.
You took jobs on the drums too, I think?
Yeah, yeah, taking jobs on the drums, yeah.
Who'd you work with? Anybody that you know of?
Yeah, yeah. I don't know if you know him, but I work on drums with a fella by the name of Luis Domain, and I also work with him on piano.
Yeah, I knew him.
Uh-huh, and I also work with Chris Kelly, one of them old times, you know. On drums and them? No, on piano. Yeah. I put the drums down there, because I got hired more on piano, you know what I mean?
George Williams said he worked with Chris on drums. Yeah, he did.

Was he with you the same time? No, George wasn't, I didn't play with Chris. Chris was playing at the Bull at that time when George was playing with him. Yeah, I remember that. He played with Chris. And I also work with Buddy Petit on a boat they call a Susquehanna.
Oh, where'd that go?
Yeah, that left from out at West End. Oh, on the lake? On the lake, and they go for his Miamiville. Yeah.
And Buddy Petit played on it? Yeah, Buddy Petit played on it.

What kind of band did he have? He had a jazz band. How big was it? Yeah, a jazz band. Who else was in it? Buddy Petit and a fella by the name of Buddy Manatee. Oh yeah, the band. He's from over the lake, yeah. You know that boy by the name. Oral Foster played with him. You might know Oral Foster, he's a drummer. Is that one they call Chinese?
No, not Chinese.

Chinese used to play with Papa Celestein years ago. Yeah, his name is Foster, don't you? Yeah, Oral Foster. What's his first name? I never did know nothing but Chinese. I never did know nothing but Chinese. I never did know a thing but Chinese. I never did know anything but Chinese. I never did know anything but Chinese. I never did know anything but Chinese. Chinese. And I also played with Luis DuMaine out at the Bungalow. That was out at the West End too. Meet Luis DuMaine and a fella by the name of, I can't think of his name. Anyway, the boy no name Wilkin playing drum, and Tom Parker playing saxophone, and a fella called Gabriel, played banjo. And Joe Watson, that's the one I was trying to think. He's a saxophone player in the clan that played Joe Watson. He's dead now though. Yeah, he's dead. Then I used to play a lot of house parties by myself too, on piano, yeah. A lot of house parties. I used to play for the superintendent of the Lane's Cotton Mill, Mr. Rickman. I used to play at his house lots of times.
I wonder what kind of parties were the, some of the white folks parties?
Yeah, white people parties, yeah.

I wonder did you ever play, they had also parties like fish and fish. And then rent, did they ever have any rent parties here much? Up in Chicago, when everybody's rent would come due to, during the Depression they'd put on a party, you know.

A lot of people used to give parties like that, we used to call them house parties. House parties. That's right, yeah, that's right, house parties. They used to give fish fries to help yourself out, you know, fish on Saturday nights like that. And they'd hire pianists then for that. They hire pianist players, that's right.
Everybody would contribute a little bit.

That's right, that's right. They'd have a torchlight on the outside to let people know it was a fish fry. A torchlight with a lantern with a candle in it, you see. And when you pass and see that light, you know it's a fish fry. That was a sign, that's right. That was a sign, that's right.
What kind of a torchlight?
It's a paper, it's paper. You can light the candle.
You can light the candle.
Okay, we were asking about the style of piano you played for instance with Chris Kelly or Buddy Petit. Yeah. If you'd use that vamp style of both hands going one on the first and the second piano.

Yeah, that's right. Just like that. That's right. Just like that. That's one time. Then sometimes you… Sometimes both hands together. Both hands, yeah. Both hands, yeah. Four, four times, according to calling. That's right. And at that time when you're playing drum most of the trumpet players, see everything was built around the trumpet at that time, you know what I mean? And most everything you played the trumpet, two licks on your bass drum, boom boom, then they started. That's right.
But that two on your bass drum, you mean the drummer would give that to someone?

Yeah, yeah. He'd give that to, I mean like you said you're going to play Panama Ray, all right. And he'd say, you know the panel record, da da da da da da da da da. Well before he started panel records he'd say, the drummer started off, boom boom, then the trumpet, da da da da da da da da da. Boom boom, da da da da da da da da. Boom boom, da da da da da da da. That's what I mean.
I thought many of you would stomp in places stomping off, giving you two beats of the bass
drum.
No, no, no, no. To reach over and hit on the bass drum or something. I wasn't sure.
The trumpet player would always knock the band off. He'd give you two licks with his feet like that and he'd knock the band off and then you'd pick up.
Did the trumpet player ever stop playing hardly during a number? Or did he keep going all the time?
Well, he would play pretty much a long time. If he lay out, he didn't lay out very long. want to beat-
